core: What a professional code of ethics is: a profession's own statement of values, principles, and standards, adopted and enforced by professional associations and frequently incorporated by reference into state licensing rules
What a code is not: not criminal law, not a complete decision procedure, and not a guarantee that following it resolves every case
The distinction between aspirational principles and enforceable standards, shown across the APA, ACA, NASW, and NOHS codes

Core values that recur across helping-profession codes: service, social justice, dignity and worth of the person, importance of human relationships, integrity, and competence (NASW), and the parallel counseling values and principles (ACA)
Ethical dilemma (two or more defensible obligations conflict) versus ethical violation (conduct falls below an enforceable standard) versus personal discomfort with a defensible course of action
Self-determination and its limits, including the serious/foreseeable/imminent risk condition used in social work
Informed consent: what must be explained, ongoing nature, capacity and assent, third-party permission, and mandated or involuntary clients
Competence and scope of practice: services only within education, training, licensure, supervision, and experience; referral and consultation when outside it
Conflict of interest: declining or managing a role when outside interests could impair objectivity or expose a client to harm or exploitation
Duties owed to multiple parties at once (client, family, employer, funder, court, community) as the structural source of most dilemmas, including 'who is the client' in third-party referrals
A structured ethical decision-making process as a way to reason and document, not a formula that outputs answers
Codes differ by profession and state licensure law governs practice (U.S. jurisdiction)
Mandated reporting and duty-to-protect obligations as legal duties that vary by state and constrain confidentiality
supporting: Consultation and supervision as an expected step when facing a dilemma
Codes address conflicts between ethics and law, and between ethics and organizational/employer demands
Avoiding imposition of the practitioner's personal values on clients
The regulatory structure: legislatures pass practice acts, boards write rules and enforce them, license titles and requirements differ by jurisdiction
outOfScope: HIPAA and 42 CFR Part 2 in depth (owned by the confidentiality-and-privacy topic in this unit)
Dual and multiple relationships, boundary crossings versus boundary violations, self-disclosure, gifts (owned by the professional-boundaries topic in this unit)
Individualized legal, ethical, clinical, or supervisory advice about any real situation
State-by-state statutory detail on reporting or duty to protect
Licensing exam preparation content and specific board disciplinary procedures

claims.claim: The NASW Code of Ethics names six core values as the basis of the profession's mission: service, social justice, dignity and worth of the person, importance of human relationships, integrity, and competence. Its most recent revision was in 2021.

The NASW Code states that it does not provide rules prescribing how social workers should act in all situations, that some of its standards are enforceable guidelines while others are aspirational, and that violating a standard in the Code does not automatically imply legal liability or violation of the law. NASW maintains formal adjudication procedures for complaints against members.

The APA Ethics Code draws an explicit line between aspirational and enforceable material: the Preamble and the five General Principles (Beneficence and Nonmaleficence, Fidelity and Responsibility, Integrity, Justice, Respect for People's Rights and Dignity) are aspirational and are not themselves enforceable rules and should not form the basis for imposing sanctions, while the Ethical Standards set out enforceable rules of conduct. The current version was adopted in 2002 and amended in 2010 and 2016, effective January 1, 2017.

Codes differ by profession. The ACA Code of Ethics (2014) names five core professional values of counseling and six fundamental principles (autonomy, nonmaleficence, beneficence, justice, fidelity, veracity) and organizes standards into nine sections; the NASW Code organizes standards into six sections of responsibilities (to clients, colleagues, in practice settings, as professionals, to the profession, and to the broader society); the NOHS Ethical Standards for Human Services Professionals (2024) organize standards by responsibility to the public and society, clients, employers, colleagues, students, the profession, and self.

Social work practice in the United States is governed by state and provincial statutes: legislatures pass the practice acts that empower regulatory boards to issue licenses and enforce practice standards, and boards write the implementing rules. Every state and province has its own licensure requirements and maintains its own statutes and rules; licensure candidates must hold an accredited degree, pass the appropriate licensing exam, and meet jurisdiction-set character requirements. Social workers are required to abide by their board's standards of conduct in addition to the profession's code.

The NASW Code provides that social workers' responsibility to the larger society or specific legal obligations may on limited occasions supersede the loyalty owed to clients, and that clients should be advised of this; mandatory reporting of child abuse is given as an example.

Self-determination is not absolute in social work ethics: the NASW Code permits limiting a client's right to self-determination when the client's actions or potential actions pose a serious, foreseeable, and imminent risk to the client or to others.

Informed consent in helping-profession codes is an ongoing, documented process covering the nature, purposes, risks, limits, and alternatives of services, the practitioner's qualifications, fees, and the limits of confidentiality; where a client cannot give voluntary consent, practitioners seek the client's assent, include the client in decisions as appropriate, and seek permission from a legally responsible third party; clients receiving mandated or involuntary services must be told the limits on confidentiality and the consequences of refusing services.

Competence in these codes is bounded: practitioners provide services only within the boundaries of their education, training, supervised experience, licensure, consultation, and professional experience, and human service professionals practice only within their expertise and scope of practice, recognizing the limits of their knowledge and skills.

Conflict of interest is defined in the APA Ethics Code by its effect: psychologists refrain from taking on a professional role when personal, scientific, professional, legal, financial, or other interests or relationships could reasonably be expected to impair their objectivity, competence, or effectiveness, or to expose the person or organization served to harm or exploitation.

Codes anticipate obligations running to more than one party. The APA Ethics Code requires that when services are provided at the request of a third party, the practitioner clarify at the outset the nature of the relationship, the practitioner's role, who the client is, the probable uses of the information, and the fact that confidentiality may be limited; it also addresses conflicts between ethics and law (1.02) and between ethics and organizational demands (1.03). The NOHS standards direct professionals to honor commitments to employers while working with all involved to manage conflicts between employer and client responsibilities. The ACA Code directs counselors who face a conflict between ethics and law to make their commitment to the code known and take steps to resolve the conflict.

Ethical decision-making models are structured reasoning processes, not answer generators: the ACA Code directs counselors facing a dilemma to use and document a model that may include consultation, consideration of relevant standards, principles, and laws, generation of potential courses of action, deliberation of risks and benefits, and selection of a course based on the circumstances and the welfare of all involved. Open-textbook treatments describe the same common steps and emphasize consultation, adherence to standards, and documentation throughout.

Mandated reporting is a legal duty created by state statute under a federal floor: the Child Abuse Prevention and Treatment Act requires each state to have provisions requiring certain individuals to report known or suspected child abuse and neglect. As of May 2023, approximately 46 states, the District of Columbia, American Samoa, Guam, the Northern Mariana Islands, and the U.S. Virgin Islands designated specific professions as mandated reporters, while Indiana, New Jersey, North Carolina, and Wyoming instead require all persons to report; social workers were designated in 41 states, the District of Columbia, and those same four territories. The circumstances that trigger a report vary from state to state.

Duty-to-warn and duty-to-protect obligations also vary by state. Following Tarasoff v. Regents of the University of California (1976), nearly every state enacted duty-to-warn or duty-to-protect provisions; NCSL's fifty-state review classifies jurisdictions as imposing a mandatory duty, a permissive authorization to disclose, or no duty, and states differ in the trigger, in which professions are covered, and in what actions discharge the duty.
Codes direct practitioners to seek consultation or supervision when facing complex ethical or legal dilemmas rather than resolving them alone.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How many U.S. states impose a mandatory duty to warn or protect
positions: Secondary summaries circulate specific counts such as 34 mandatory, 13 permissive, and 4 silent

NCSL's own brief and fifty-state chart, last updated March 16, 2022, classify jurisdictions as mandatory, permissive, or no duty but the counts depend on how multi-statute states and territories are tallied
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states the qualitative pattern NCSL supports (most states require or permit disclosure, a small number impose no duty, and the trigger and covered professions differ) and does not publish a precise count. Precise counts are time-sensitive and vary by counting method.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether a code of ethics is legally binding
positions: The NASW Code states that violating a standard does not automatically imply legal liability or a violation of law
Many state boards adopt or reference a professional code in rule, so the same conduct can also breach a licensing regulation
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Both are true and are taught together: the code is enforced by the profession, while legal consequences flow from statute and board rule. The lesson does not claim that any particular state has adopted any particular code, because adoption varies by jurisdiction.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft contained no substantive claims about ethics at all; its body text was generic placeholder prose about 'a foundational concept' that could have described any topic.

The draft's vocabulary list defined the topic circularly ('a foundational Social Work & Human Services concept covered in this lesson') and offered generic entries for context, evidence, and application rather than the operative ethics vocabulary.
The draft's quick-check items tested generic study skills rather than any ethics content and had only three options each.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced all placeholder prose with sourced content on codes, values, dilemmas, self-determination, consent, competence, conflicts of interest, multi-party duties, and decision processes.
Added the accuracy points the draft lacked: codes differ by profession, state licensure law governs practice, and mandated reporting and duty-to-protect are legal duties that vary by state.
Added an explicit statement that the lesson is educational material and not legal advice, clinical direction, or supervision.
Rebuilt the question bank to five four-option items with difficulty, skill, explanation, and source attribution.
rightsIssues: The NASW Code of Ethics is copyrighted (© National Association of Social Workers). It is used REFERENCE_ONLY: its content is described and summarized in original wording and no standard text is reproduced.

The ACA Code of Ethics (© 2014 American Counseling Association) and the APA Ethical Principles of Psychologists and Code of Conduct (© American Psychological Association) are likewise copyrighted and used REFERENCE_ONLY.
The NOHS Ethical Standards (© 2024 National Organization for Human Services) permit non-commercial reproduction only in their entirety; treated as REFERENCE_ONLY and paraphrased.
The Child Welfare Information Gateway publication states it may be freely reproduced and distributed with credit; recorded as ATTRIBUTION_REQUIRED. Facts were extracted and rewritten regardless.

The University of Minnesota open textbook is CC BY 4.0; recorded as ATTRIBUTION_REQUIRED. No sentences were adapted from it — it was used to confirm the shape of decision-making models and code structures.
NCSL content is © National Conference of State Legislatures; used REFERENCE_ONLY for the fifty-state pattern.
No source prose appears in the lesson. All lesson wording is original.

sourceRecords.title: NASW Code of Ethics (2021 revision), including Ethical Responsibilities to Clients
sourceRecords.notes: Primary source for the six core values, the Code's six stated purposes, the aspirational-versus-enforceable distinction, the statement that the Code does not prescribe conduct for all situations, the statement that violating a standard does not automatically imply legal liability, the six sections of ethical standards, and standards 1.01-1.04 (commitment to clients, self-determination and the serious/foreseeable/imminent risk limit, informed consent and capacity, competence). Copyrighted; described in original wording only, no text reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: 2014 ACA Code of Ethics
sourceRecords.notes: Source for counseling's five core professional values and six fundamental principles (autonomy, nonmaleficence, beneficence, justice, fidelity, veracity), the Code's six purposes and nine sections, A.2 informed consent including types of information, developmental and cultural sensitivity, inability to give consent, and mandated clients, A.4.b personal values, I.1.b ethical decision making, and I.1.c conflicts between ethics and laws. Copyrighted; paraphrased only.

sourceRecords.title: Ethical Principles of Psychologists and Code of Conduct (2002, amended 2010 and 2016; effective January 1, 2017)
sourceRecords.notes: Source for the explicit aspirational-versus-enforceable distinction, the five General Principles, Standard 1.02 (conflicts between ethics and law) and 1.03 (conflicts between ethics and organizational demands), 2.01 boundaries of competence, 3.06 conflict of interest defined by impairment or exposure to harm, and 3.07 third-party requests for services and clarifying who the client is. Copyrighted; paraphrased only.

sourceRecords.title: Ethical Standards for Human Services Professionals (adopted 2024)
sourceRecords.notes: Source for the human services profession having its own code organized by responsibility domains (public and society, clients, employers, colleagues, students, profession, self), Standard 2 informed consent including clients unable to consent and mandated services, Standard 4 safety-based disclosure in accordance with state and federal law, Standard 12 duty to be informed about relevant law, Standard 24 managing employer-versus-client conflicts, Standard 26 scope of practice, and Standard 28 consultation and supervision in dilemmas. Reproduction permitted only in entirety for non-commercial use; treated as reference only.

sourceRecords.title: Rules for licensure
sourceRecords.notes: Source for the regulatory structure: statutes governing social work licensing are passed by state and provincial legislatures, those statutes empower boards to issue licenses and enforce practice standards, boards implement rules for practice, and social workers are required to abide by their board's standards of conduct in addition to the profession's code. Also supports that licensure requirements include an accredited degree, examination, and jurisdiction-set character requirements, and that ASWB links to every state and province's own statutes and rules. The related overview page at https://www.aswb.org/licenses/ states that every state and province has its own requirements for getting a license; that page was checked on the same date.
